plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked schematic of Cajal's Law of Dynamic Polarization (dendrites → soma → axon → 20 nm synaptic cleft → next dendrite) sits alongside a resolution chart comparing 19th-century light microscopes (200 nm blur limit) against 1954–1955 electron microscopy (0.2 nm resolution directly photographing the 20 nm synaptic cleft and vesicles).

teach_overlay.label: DYNAMIC POLARIZATION & 1954 ELECTRON MICROSCOPE (20 NM CLEFT VS 200 NM LIGHT LIMIT)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked diagram on period paper of Cajal's Law of Dynamic Polarization (dendrites → soma → axon → 20 nm synaptic cleft → next dendrite) alongside 1954–1955 electron microscopy resolution (0.2 nm resolving the 20 nm cleft vs 200 nm light limit)
teach_overlay.scale: nineteenth-century light microscopes blurred anything smaller than 200 nanometres — ten times wider than the 20-nanometre synaptic gap, which is why only Cajal's embryonic silver stains and 1950s electron microscopes could prove the gap was real
